newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin's wilfulness is bad for his health.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin's wilfulness is bad for his health.

text.p: The energy and obstinacy which helped Boris Yeltsin overpower more than 70 years of communism are proving something of a liability now that his heart is failing him.

Instead of resting before the cardiac surgery he has said he will have at the end of the month, Yeltsin went hunting and fishing, to the dismay of the surgeon who has been chosen to do the bypass operation.
His daughter Tatyana said doctors had since managed to get her father into hospital and keep him there, but only just.
"We had to make a big effort to persuade him to remain in the Central Clinical Hospital," she told Russian television on Sunday.
"He is a very active person and to stay shut up in a room is for him, well, a mortal danger," she said with a laugh.

Yeltsin was reported to have shot more than 40 ducks and a wild boar during hunting trips during the week of September 5, when he told the nation he needed a heart operation to allow him to return to normal life.
He was shooting so much a special cushion had to be made to stop him bruising his shoulder, a Kremlin source told Reuters.
"I was not very pleased with it, because he had got tired... For a sick person in such a situation it is not a very good idea, it's a burden," said cardiac surgeon Renat Akchurin.
Akchurin, worried that Yeltsin may not survive the operation, said on Sunday it might have to be postponed for up to two months or even called off altogether.
But, having steeled himself for the ordeal, Yeltsin wants to get on with it, Akchurin told NTV commercial television.

"The president is pushing us but we are all insisting quite firmly that we need to go through a certain preparatory period...An early operation in the circumstances clearly carries a bigger risk," he said.
Doctors will decide on Wednesday whether Yeltsin's health is good enough to withstand the operation. If they decide it is not, they have a problem on their hands.

"We would be forced to limit his physical activies. From what I know of him...he would not tolerate this," Akchurin said. "He can work mentally, sure, but physically this whole thing has limited him."
Earlier this year, Yeltsin, who led resistance to an attempted hardline coup in 1991, faced a communist challenge to his Kremlin post.
Stirring himself from almost two years of lethargy -- he has admitted that he can be apathetic when not under pressure -- Yeltsin went to the opposite extreme.
He put two heart attacks behind him and criss-crossed the world's biggest country, meeting the people, dancing and swinging on a swing to prove he was fit.
Akchurin said this had taken its toll, probably prompting a third attack just before the election runoff in July and making a long recovery period essential before he could have surgery.
But the determination in the face of adversity which drove his rise to power and helped him win a second term may yet be the decisive factor which sees Yeltsin through.
Tatyana said she was sure he was worried by the operation, although he gave no signs of concern. "He doesn't show it..he's such a strong person that he keeps everything inside," she said.
Akchurin said Yeltsin was in a "fighting mood" and that this always seemed to help with heart bypass patients.
He added with a chuckle that Yeltsin had turned the tables on him by assuming the role of comforter, saying: "You don't have to worry, I'll walk out of here."
